post.title: Why You Forget Things You Just Googled #shorts
post.description: What do you always re-Google? Tell me in the comments. Send this to the friend who Googles the same thing twice. Milo googled how long to boil an egg. Third time this week. In 'Google Effects on Memory: Cognitive Consequences of Having Information at Our Fingertips' (Science, 2011), Betsy Sparrow, Jenny Liu and Daniel Wegner had people type trivia statements into a computer. Those told the computer would save them remembered the statements less well than those told they'd be erased. In another experiment, people were better at remembering where a fact was saved than the fact itself. The idea: when we expect to be able to look something up, we treat the device as an outside memory. Fair caveat: one part of the paper (a reaction-time test) didn't replicate in a large 2018 replication project, so treat this as a tendency, not a law. #psychology #shorts #memory #google #overthinking

lines.text: Milo GOOGLED boiled egg time. Third time this week.
You've done it: looked it up yesterday, GONE today.
But your memory isn't broken. It's being EFFICIENT.
In 2011, Betsy Sparrow's team had people type trivia FACTS.

lines.text: Told the computer would save them, they remembered LESS.
But they remembered WHERE it was saved.
Psychologists call it the GOOGLE effect.
Think of something you've Googled more than ONCE. Yeah, that one.
Your brain didn't forget. It filed it under 'PHONE.' What do you always re-Google? Send this to the friend who Googles the same thing twice.
